action_criteria.expected_evidence: Give-way leg weakness, left Hoover sign, distractible gait and tremor; a witnessed event with eyes closed and preserved responsiveness
action_criteria.label: Examine for positive functional signs
action_criteria.rationale: The examination establishes the functional leg weakness (collapsing weakness, Hoover sign, distractibility) and, because an event occurred in front of the examiner, documents a semiology typical of functional seizures.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Sodium 134 mEq/L with osmolality 278 mOsm/kg, too mild to provoke seizures
action_criteria.label: Serum sodium and osmolality
action_criteria.rationale: He drinks 7-8 L a day and had a hyponatremic seizure 18 months ago; a sodium answers whether the events could be provoked before they are attributed to anything else.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Habitual events recorded on video with no EEG change and a normal interictal record
action_criteria.label: Video-EEG to record the habitual events
action_criteria.rationale: Recording the habitual events on video-EEG without ictal change reaches the ILAE documented level of certainty and screens for co-occurring epilepsy, which a prior provoked seizure, risperidone and a family history keep in question (AAN 2025). Without the recording, the positive signs and the semiology of witnessed events support the diagnosis at a lower ILAE level of certainty (LaFrance 2013).

action_criteria.label: 12-lead ECG
action_criteria.rationale: The events were first reported as loss of consciousness and risperidone can prolong QT; an ECG is defensible but does not bear on the diagnosis.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Risperidone's small seizure-threshold effect, hyperprolactinemia and hyponatremia risk; haloperidol contraindicated
action_criteria.label: Medication review
action_criteria.rationale: Risperidone bears on the seizure threshold, prolactin and sodium, benztropine on thirst, and his haloperidol reaction on any future antipsychotic choice; the review informs the plan, not the diagnosis.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Profile of comorbid mood, anxiety and somatic symptom burden to guide therapy; no bearing on the diagnosis
action_criteria.label: Neuropsychological assessment of mood, anxiety and dissociation
action_criteria.rationale: A battery with performance-validity measures can characterise the comorbidity that treatment will target; it does not make the diagnosis and is the most expensive item on this pathway.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Background evidence only; the diagnosis and plan for this patient do not depend on a literature result
action_criteria.label: Search the literature on functional neurological disorder
action_criteria.rationale: General evidence on positive diagnosis and treatment can inform the explanation and the referral; no step of the diagnostic work-up depends on it.

prohibited_recommendations: Order further investigations once the positive diagnosis is established, without a new specific clinical question (repeat MRI, CT, lumbar puncture, EMG or nerve conduction studies, evoked potentials, PET).
Tell the patient the symptoms are imagined, feigned, 'all in your head', or that nothing is wrong.
Perform invasive testing without a specific indication (lumbar puncture, nerve or muscle biopsy, catheter angiography).
Start or escalate antiseizure medication for the functional seizures.
Give benzodiazepines or intubate for a typical functional seizure.
Give gadolinium contrast without a specific indication.
required_recommendations: Make a positive diagnosis of functional neurological disorder (mixed: functional seizures and functional leg weakness) based on collapsing leg weakness, a left Hoover sign and distractibility, and the semiology of the habitual events, confirmed on video-EEG where recorded, and not by exclusion of other disease.

Explain the diagnosis to the patient, and with consent to the family, as a common and genuine disorder of nervous system functioning that can improve, show the positive signs, and give written information, together with his psychiatric team.
Refer for physiotherapy with expertise in functional motor disorder (motor retraining, Nielsen 2015 consensus).
Refer for psychological therapy by a clinician experienced in FND (CBT-informed) and treat the comorbid anxiety, with therapy adapted to his schizophrenia and coordinated with his psychiatrist.

Give the patient, family and ward a written plan for typical events: keep safe, do not restrain, wait for the event to end, and do not give emergency benzodiazepines or intubate for a typical functional seizure.
Continue risperidone at the current dose with his psychiatrist, and manage the polydipsia with monitored fluid intake and periodic sodium checks.

avoided_actions.rationale: No murmur, cardiac symptom or syncopal feature; the events keep responsiveness and recover at once.
The events keep responsiveness and recover at once, without syncopal features; a rhythm recording answers no question.
No head injury, focal sign or reflex change; a CT answers no question raised by the events or the weakness.
Afebrile, no encephalopathy and a normal EEG background; a lumbar puncture is invasive and answers no question.
FDG-PET has no role in events recorded without ictal change or in functional weakness.
Collapsing weakness, a Hoover sign and normal reflexes answer the weakness question; EMG and nerve conduction studies would only reinforce the search for an organic cause.
The shifting stocking sensory boundary is not a pathway lesion; evoked potentials answer no question.

accepted: Functional neurological symptom disorder (conversion disorder) with mixed symptoms — psychogenic non-epileptic seizures (PNES) and functional limb weakness

differential.key_features: Habitual events recorded on video-EEG without ictal change; co-occurring epilepsy remains possible in about one in five patients with functional seizures, and risperidone and a maternal uncle with epilepsy are noted.
Polydipsia of 7-8 L a day and a prior hyponatremic seizure, but sodium is 134 mEq/L with osmolality 278 mOsm/kg, too mild to provoke seizures, and the events show no ictal change.
Mild wrist rigidity on risperidone, but the tremor varies in amplitude and frequency, increases with attention and diminishes during mental arithmetic, which a drug-induced tremor does not do.

Difficulty rising and climbing stairs suggests a proximal pattern, but the weakness collapses with effort, the Hoover sign is positive, bulk is normal and leg strength is preserved when he stands to reach.

key_clinical_evidence: An event witnessed on examination: asynchronous arm trembling with side-to-side head movement, eyes tightly closed, responsive throughout, immediate recovery.
Video-EEG recorded four habitual events, one from apparent sleep with a waking background, all without ictal change.
Sodium 134 mEq/L and osmolality 278 mOsm/kg: polydipsia has not produced a hyponatremia that could provoke seizures.
Leg weakness with collapsing strength, a left Hoover sign and a gait that improves with dual tasking; reflexes are normal.
Schizophrenia, the job loss and adolescent trauma are context and treatment targets, neither required nor sufficient for the diagnosis.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: It makes a sodium the first test; at 134 mEq/L it cannot provoke seizures, and the events are recorded without ictal change.
red_herrings.data_point: Polydipsia with a hyponatremic seizure 18 months ago
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attributing the events to recurrent hyponatremia without checking the sodium, or after a mildly low result
red_herrings.location: Past medical history and history of present illness

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A second-degree relative with epilepsy barely changes his risk; the semiology of the habitual events decides, and a video-EEG recording confirms it.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchoring on epilepsy and starting antiseizure medication before the events are recorded

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: FND can coexist with psychosis; it is diagnosed by the same positive signs and event semiology.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Diagnostic overshadowing: attributing the events and weakness to the psychotic illness or its medication

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Trauma and stressors are common in FND but neither necessary nor sufficient; the signs and the event semiology make the diagnosis.
red_herrings.data_point: Witnessed mother's death at 16; recent job loss
red_herrings.intended_effect: Treating trauma or stress as proof of FND without verifying positive signs

findings.result: Hip flexors collapse from 4/5 to 1/5 and knee extensors from 4/5 to 2/5 with sustained effort, bilaterally.
Left hip extension weak on direct testing, full during right hip flexion against resistance.
Gait improves during dual-task walking, left heel-shin wavering lessens with conversation, and the hand tremor diminishes during mental arithmetic.

A 70-second episode of asynchronous arm trembling with side-to-side head movement and eyes tightly closed, verbally responsive throughout, with immediate recovery; a 20-second right arm episode when his job loss was discussed.

Bilateral foot-dragging gait with exaggerated sway but no fall, excessive effort rising from a chair with preserved strength when reaching while standing, and a shifting stocking sensory boundary sparing the soles; not counted as rule-in signs.
Mild wrist rigidity bilaterally; reflexes 2+ and symmetric, flexor plantar responses.

clinical_assessment.impression: Positive signs of functional weakness: collapsing weakness of both legs, a left Hoover sign and distractibility. The pattern is inconsistent with a structural lesion. The event semiology (eyes closed, asynchronous movements, side-to-side head movement, preserved responsiveness, immediate recovery) is typical of functional seizures; the examination does not by itself exclude epileptic seizures.

contraindications: Haloperidol: documented acute dystonic reaction; avoid high-potency first-generation antipsychotics.
general.proposed: Risperidone 2 mg once daily at bedtime; Benztropine 1 mg twice daily; Melatonin 3 mg nightly
general.summary: No interacting pair. Risperidone slightly lowers the seizure threshold and raises prolactin; antipsychotics and polydipsia predispose to hyponatremia; benztropine dries the mouth. Haloperidol is contraindicated by allergy.
warnings: Risperidone: small, dose-related lowering of the seizure threshold; low risk at 2 mg daily.
Risperidone: hyperprolactinemia is common and makes a post-event prolactin uninterpretable.
Antipsychotics are associated with hyponatremia, particularly with primary polydipsia; monitor sodium.
Benztropine: anticholinergic dry mouth can increase fluid intake; confusion and constipation.

activating_procedures.hyperventilation: Performed on day 1; no abnormalities. No clinical event provoked.
activating_procedures.photic_stimulation: Normal photic driving; no photoparoxysmal response.
activating_procedures.sleep_deprivation: Relative sleep deprivation on night 2; no interictal epileptiform discharges emerged.

The EEG showed a waking background with a reactive posterior dominant rhythm immediately before and throughout the event; no ictal pattern; no postictal slowing or suppression.

eeg.impression: This is a NORMAL video-EEG. 4 habitual events were recorded (asynchronous shaking of all four limbs with eyes closed; bilateral arm tremor with head shaking while responsive; whole-body shaking arising from apparent sleep with a waking background; isolated right arm shaking) without ictal EEG change before, during or after the events; the posterior dominant rhythm persisted during the events. No interictal epileptiform discharges. No electrographic seizures.
eeg.limitations: Movement artifact during events partially obscured frontal and temporal channels, but posterior channels were consistently interpretable.

labs.interpretation: Sodium 134 mEq/L (low). Remaining results within reference ranges.

results.finding: Diagnosis of functional neurological disorder rests on positive clinical features such as the Hoover sign, tremor entrainment and functional seizure semiology, not on the exclusion of other disease; treatment combines explanation, physiotherapy and psychological therapy.
results.source: Espay AJ et al. JAMA Neurol 2018;75:1132-1141

results.finding: Motor signs such as the Hoover sign, hip abductor sign, drift without pronation and dragging gait have high specificity; sensory signs such as midline splitting have low specificity.
results.source: Daum C et al. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2014;85:180-190

results.finding: Defines levels of certainty for psychogenic nonepileptic seizures; the documented level requires a typical event recorded on video-EEG without ictal EEG change.
results.source: LaFrance WC Jr et al. Epilepsia 2013;54:2005-2018

results.finding: For functional seizures: assess for co-occurring epilepsy and psychiatric disorders, taper antiseizure medication without another indication, avoid benzodiazepines, and offer psychological therapy, which is possibly effective.
CBT added to standardised medical care did not reduce dissociative seizure frequency at 12 months; several secondary outcomes favoured CBT.
results.source: Goldstein LH et al. Lancet Psychiatry 2020;7:491-505

results.finding: Specialist physiotherapy for functional motor disorder was not superior to community neurological physiotherapy on physical function at 12 months; several secondary outcomes favoured it.
results.source: Nielsen G et al. Lancet Neurol 2024;23:675-686

results.finding: About 4% of patients diagnosed with conversion symptoms since 1970 later received another diagnosis.

functional neurological disorder diagnos.summary: Guideline and trial evidence supports a positive clinical diagnosis of functional neurological disorder, video-EEG confirmation of functional seizures, tapering of unneeded antiseizure drugs and benzodiazepines, and physiotherapy and psychological treatment whose trial effects on primary outcomes were modest.

clinical_pearls: Hoover sign: hip extension of the weak leg is weak on direct testing but returns to full strength during flexion of the opposite hip against resistance; a reliable positive sign of functional weakness
Tremor entrainment: functional tremor changes frequency or is disrupted by voluntary rhythmic movements of another limb; also diminishes with distraction (mental arithmetic)
Eyes tightly closed during a seizure-like event is more common in PNES than in epileptic seizures
Post-event prolactin is unreliable in patients on dopamine-blocking antipsychotics like risperidone due to baseline hyperprolactinemia
Hyponatremia-induced seizures typically occur at sodium levels below 120 mEq/L; mild hyponatremia (130-135) rarely if ever causes seizures
Diagnostic overshadowing: the tendency to attribute all symptoms to an existing diagnosis (e.g., schizophrenia) and miss comorbid conditions like FND
metadata.difficulty_description: Moderate difficulty due to multiple confounding factors: (1) history of a true prior hyponatremia-induced seizure creating expectation bias, (2) current mild hyponatremia serving as a red herring, (3) risperidone confounding prolactin interpretation, (4) comorbid schizophrenia risking diagnostic overshadowing, and (5) family history of epilepsy. However, positive functional signs on examination and EEG findings are present to guide diagnosis.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Functional seizures and leg weakness in a man with schizophrenia, polydipsia and a prior hyponatremic seizure: the agent should check the sodium, find the positive signs, recognise the event semiology and avoid diagnostic overshadowing.

patient.history_present_illness:
Mr. Anwar is a 38-year-old right-handed man with a 19-year history of paranoid schizophrenia, stable on risperidone 2 mg daily, who is brought to the emergency department by his father after two episodes of generalized shaking with apparent loss of consciousness earlier today. His father reports that the first episode occurred in the morning while the patient was sitting in the living room watching television. The patient suddenly slumped forward and developed bilateral shaking of all four extremities lasting approximately two minutes. His father noted that the patient's eyes were tightly shut throughout the episode and that the shaking appeared irregular and asynchronous between the limbs. The patient did not bite his tongue and there was no urinary incontinence. When the shaking stopped, the patient appeared immediately alert and was able to speak without confusion, though he appeared emotionally distressed and tearful.

A second episode occurred approximately three hours later while the patient was eating lunch. His father describes similar bilateral arm and leg shaking lasting roughly 90 seconds, again with eyes closed. The patient appeared to respond to his name being called during this episode by nodding his head slightly. Recovery was again rapid with no post-event confusion or drowsiness. The father called emergency services after this second event.

On further history, the patient reports that similar episodes have been occurring intermittently over the past three months, approximately once or twice per week, though today is the first time two events have occurred on the same day. The episodes vary in duration from 30 seconds to three minutes. He denies any consistent aura or warning symptom, though he notes that the episodes tend to occur during periods of emotional distress. He has been increasingly anxious since losing his job six months ago and reports feeling like a burden to his father.

The patient has a documented history of psychogenic polydipsia with a prior episode of hyponatremia-induced seizure 18 months ago. His father reports that the patient's water intake had increased again in recent weeks, estimating approximately 7-8 liters per day, which raised concern for recurrent hyponatremia as the cause of the current episodes. The patient acknowledges excessive water intake but states he feels compelled to drink.

In addition to the episodic shaking events, the patient reports progressive weakness in both legs that began approximately three months ago. He first noticed difficulty rising from a seated position and climbing stairs, and the weakness has gradually worsened such that he now walks with difficulty and requires assistance for longer distances. He denies back pain, bowel or bladder dysfunction, or preceding trauma. His father notes that the weakness seems to fluctuate, with the patient occasionally walking more normally when he is distracted or engaged in an activity he enjoys. The patient also reports intermittent trembling of his hands that worsens when people are watching him. He has been increasingly socially withdrawn and expresses concern that he is developing a brain disease. His uncle's history of epilepsy has heightened his fear that he has developed seizures.

neurological_exam.additional: During the examination, the patient had a witnessed episode of bilateral upper extremity trembling and head shaking lasting approximately 70 seconds, with eyes tightly closed and side-to-side head movements. The patient was verbally responsive during the event, answering 'yes' when asked if he could hear the examiner. No tongue biting, no urinary incontinence. The tremor was asynchronous between the two arms. No post-event confusion or drowsiness; the patient was immediately conversant after the event ceased. A second brief episode of right arm shaking lasting 20 seconds occurred 15 minutes later when the topic of his recent job loss was discussed.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose intact bilaterally without dysmetria. Heel-to-shin performed inconsistently on the left, with exaggerated wavering that does not follow a cerebellar pattern; performance improves when the patient is distracted by conversation.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal and reactive, 3 mm to 2 mm bilaterally. Visual fields full to confrontation. Extraocular movements intact without nystagmus. No facial asymmetry at rest or with activation. Facial sensation intact bilaterally. Hearing grossly intact. Palate elevates symmetrically. Tongue midline without fasciculations. Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius strength 5/5 bilaterally.
neurological_exam.gait: The patient walks with a slow, deliberate gait, dragging both feet but more pronounced on the left. When asked to walk heel-to-toe, demonstrates dramatic truncal sway with arms outstretched but does not fall. During dual-task testing (walking while naming animals), gait pattern notably improves with more natural stride length and reduced foot dragging. Chair sign positive: uses excessive effort to rise from chair but demonstrates preserved leg strength when reaching for an offered object while standing.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person, place, and time. Speech somewhat monotonous in prosody but fluent without paraphasic errors. Affect blunted, consistent with known negative symptoms of schizophrenia. No active hallucinations or delusions elicited during examination. Naming, repetition, and comprehension intact. Recall 3/3 at registration and 2/3 at 5 minutes (recalls third with category cue). Attention intact on serial sevens. No thought disorder evident.
neurological_exam.motor: Bulk normal throughout. Tone mildly increased at the wrists bilaterally, consistent with mild antipsychotic-related rigidity. Upper extremity strength 5/5 bilaterally. In the lower extremities, the patient demonstrates give-way weakness in bilateral hip flexors (collapsing from 4/5 to 1/5 with sustained effort) and bilateral knee extensors (4/5 to 2/5). Hoover sign positive on the left: left hip extension is weak on direct testing but full during right hip flexion against resistance. No fasciculations. Intermittent coarse tremor of both upper extremities noted during examination, irregular in amplitude and frequency, which increases with attention and diminishes when the patient is asked to perform mental arithmetic.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ and symmetric at biceps, triceps, and brachioradialis bilaterally. Patellar reflexes 2+ bilaterally. Achilles reflexes 2+ bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor (downgoing) bilaterally. No clonus.
neurological_exam.sensory: Reports decreased sensation to light touch in both lower extremities below the knees in a stocking-like distribution, but testing reveals inconsistencies: the patient reports reduced sensation on the dorsum of the feet but normal sensation on the soles, and the boundary of sensory loss shifts between examinations. Vibration and proprioception intact bilaterally at the great toes. No midline splitting of truncal sensation.
